claim: Baboons comprise six closely related species distributed throughout sub-Saharan Africa and southwest Arabia.
source: Baboons, members of the genus Papio, comprise six closely related species distributed throughout sub-Saharan Africa and southwest Arabia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the distribution map in Figure 1.

claim: Baboons exhibit more ecological flexibility and a wider range of social systems than many other primates.
source: The species exhibit more ecological flexibility and a wider range of social systems than many other primates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed descriptions of ecological and social variation throughout the manuscript.

claim: The evolution of baboons has been heavily shaped by climatic changes and population expansion and fragmentation in the African savanna environment.
source: The evolution of baboons has been heavily shaped by climatic changes and population expansion and fragmentation in the African savanna environment, similar to the processes that acted during human evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogeographic analyses discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Baboon evolutionary processes are similar to those that acted during human evolution.
source: The evolution of baboons has been heavily shaped by climatic changes and population expansion and fragmentation in the African savanna environment, similar to the processes that acted during human evolution.
evidence: This comparison is explicitly stated in the abstract and elaborated in the phylogeography section.

claim: Charles Darwin remarked 'He who understands baboon would do more towards metaphysics than Locke' in 1838.
source: Humans have been captivated by baboons for thousands of years: from ancient Egypt, where the god of wisdom, Thoth, was depicted with a baboon head, to the mid-19th century when Charles Darwin remarked, "He who understands baboon would do more towards metaphysics than Locke" (Darwin, 1838).
evidence: This is a direct quote attributed to Darwin with a citation.

claim: Eugene Marais provided one of the first detailed accounts of free-ranging baboons at the beginning of the 20th century.
source: At the beginning of the 20th century, the South African naturalist Eugene Marais provided one of the first detailed accounts of free-ranging baboons (Marais, 1939)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Marais's work.

claim: Sherwood Washburn and Irven DeVore investigated baboons in Kenya in the 1950s.
source: This was the decade that the American physical anthropologist Sherwood Washburn and his student Irven DeVore set out to investigate baboons in Kenya (Vore and Washburn, 1961).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to their work.

claim: Washburn reasoned that ground-living baboons were a good model for early human adaptations because they evolved in African savannas alongside ancestral hominins.
source: Washburn reasoned that these ground-living primates were a good model for early human adaptations because they evolved in African savannas alongside ancestral hominins.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as Washburn's reasoning.

claim: The US National Institutes of Health funded a three-year proposal titled 'Initiation and Support of Colony of Baboons' in 1958.
source: Meanwhile, increasing interest in the use of non-human primates as biomedical models for humans led to the funding in 1958 of a three-year proposal titled "Initiation and Support of Colony of Baboons" by the US National Institutes of Health, with the first group of baboons shipped to the United States from Kenya in 1960 (VandeBerg, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to VandeBerg 2009.

claim: The first group of baboons was shipped to the United States from Kenya in 1960.
source: Meanwhile, increasing interest in the use of non-human primates as biomedical models for humans led to the funding in 1958 of a three-year proposal titled "Initiation and Support of Colony of Baboons" by the US National Institutes of Health, with the first group of baboons shipped to the United States from Kenya in 1960 (VandeBerg, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Baboons constitute an excellent model organism for investigating fundamental biological processes such as physiological and behavioral adaptation, hybridization and speciation with gene flow.
source: Collectively, these characteristics make baboons an excellent model organism for investigating a range of fundamental biological processes, such as physiological and behavioral adaptation, hybridization and speciation with gene flow (Alfred and Baldwin, 2015).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with a supporting citation.

claim: All extant baboons belong to the genus Papio within the tribe Papionini and family Cercopithecidae.
source: Within the primate order, all extant baboons belong to the genus Papio. The genus is part of the tribe Papionini, within the family Cercopithecidae.
evidence: This is a direct statement of taxonomic classification.

claim: Baboons originated in southern Africa according to the fossil record and phylogeographic analyses.
source: The fossil record and phylogeographic analyses indicate that baboons originated in southern Africa.
evidence: This is stated based on fossil and phylogeographic evidence.

claim: The initial divergence of baboon lineages occurred 1.5–2.1 million years ago.
source: Nuclear and mitochondrial estimates put the date of initial divergence of baboon lineages at 1.5–2.1 million years ago (Newman et al., 2004; Rogers et al., 2019; Zinner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to genetic studies.

claim: During the Pleistocene epoch, baboons started to expand their range across sub-Saharan Africa into both northern and southern savannas.
source: At about the same time, during the Pleistocene epoch, baboons started to expand their range across sub-Saharan Africa into both northern and southern savannas.
evidence: This is stated as a temporal correlation with the divergence timing.

claim: Six baboon species are currently recognized: chacma, yellow, Kinda, olive, Guinea, and hamadryas baboons.
source: Presently, six species are recognized: the chacma baboon (Papio ursinus), which is found in southern Africa; the yellow baboon (Papio cynocephalus), which inhabits large parts of eastern Africa; the Kinda baboon (Papio kindae), which is found in Zambia, eastern Angola, and southern DR Congo; the olive baboon (Papio anubis), whose distribution ranges from northern DR Congo to parts of Kenya and Tanzania across to Sierra Leone in the west and to Eritrea in the east; the Guinea baboon (Papio papio), which is found from Sierra Leone to Mauritania and Senegal; and the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas), which inhabits parts of Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and the south-western part of the Arabian peninsula (Figure 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hybrid zones are found where baboon species' distributions come into contact.
source: Hybrid zones are found where species' distributions come into contact.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: According to the biological species concept, all baboon taxa would be considered one polytypic species (Papio hamadryas) because they interbreed freely where they meet in the wild.
source: According to the biological species concept (Mayr, 1963), all taxa would be considered one polytypic species (Papio hamadryas) because where they meet in the wild they interbreed freely, producing viable and fertile hybrid offspring.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the biological species concept.

claim: The authors follow the phylogenetic species concept and refer to the different baboon taxa as 'species'.
source: Given that the different taxa vary substantially in appearance, behavior, and the characteristics of their society, we follow the phylogenetic species concept (Cracraft, 1983), and refer to the different taxa as "species".
evidence: This is an explicit methodological choice stated by the authors.

claim: All baboon species are anatomically and morphologically well adapted to a quadrupedal terrestrial lifestyle.
source: All baboon species are anatomically and morphologically well adapted to a quadrupedal terrestrial lifestyle (Fleagle, 2013).

claim: Baboons have dog-like muzzles and males have large canine teeth.
source: They have dog-like muzzles and males have large canine teeth.

claim: Adult male baboons have body mass between 17 and 30 kg depending on the species.
source: Depending on the species, body mass varies between 17 and 30 kg for adult males, and between 10 and 15 kg for females, resulting in a sexual dimorphism in mass ranging between 1.55 and 2.20 (Anandam et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2017; Swedell, 2011).

claim: Adult female baboons have body mass between 10 and 15 kg.
source: Depending on the species, body mass varies between 17 and 30 kg for adult males, and between 10 and 15 kg for females, resulting in a sexual dimorphism in mass ranging between 1.55 and 2.20 (Anandam et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2017; Swedell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Sexual dimorphism in mass in baboons ranges between 1.55 and 2.20.
source: Depending on the species, body mass varies between 17 and 30 kg for adult males, and between 10 and 15 kg for females, resulting in a sexual dimorphism in mass ranging between 1.55 and 2.20 (Anandam et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2017; Swedell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Baboon species differ notably in fur color, body size and sexually selected characteristics such as capes.
source: The species differ notably in their fur color, body size and sexually selected characteristics, such as the distinct capes which are most pronounced in Guinea and hamadryas baboons but also present in olive baboons.

claim: Capes are most pronounced in Guinea and hamadryas baboons but also present in olive baboons.
source: The species differ notably in their fur color, body size and sexually selected characteristics, such as the distinct capes which are most pronounced in Guinea and hamadryas baboons but also present in olive baboons.
evidence: This is explicitly stated.

claim: Females of all baboon species develop sexual swellings of the anogenital region when they are fertile.
source: Females of all species develop sexual swellings of the anogenital region when they are fertile.
evidence: This is stated as a universal characteristic across species.

claim: Sexual swellings change throughout the menstrual cycle such that maximum swelling typically coincides with ovulation.
source: These swelling change throughout the menstrual cycle, such that maximum swelling typically coincides with ovulation (Higham et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: The size and shape of sexual swellings varies considerably among baboon species.
source: The size and shape of the swellings varies considerably among species (Figure 2; Petersdorf et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All baboon species are largely terrestrial during the day but retreat to sleeping trees or cliffs during the night.
source: All baboon species are largely terrestrial during the day but retreat to sleeping trees or cliffs during the night.
evidence: This is stated as a universal behavioral pattern.

claim: Baboons exhibit great ecological flexibility, allowing them to occupy habitats including semi-deserts grasslands, woodland savannas, humid forests, and Afroalpine grasslands over 3,000 meters above sea level.
source: They exhibit great ecological flexibility, allowing them to occupy habitats including semi-deserts grasslands, woodland savannas, humid forests, and Afroalpine grasslands over 3,000 meters above sea level (Chala et al., 2019; Fuchs et al., 2018).

claim: Baboon diet mainly consists of plants, including fruit, seeds, leaves, and roots.
source: Baboons eat a broad range of foods, although their diet mainly consists of plants, including fruit, seeds, leaves, and roots.

claim: Baboons also eat insects and other arthropods and occasionally kill small antelopes, hares, rodents, birds and smaller monkeys.
source: They also eat insects and other arthropods and, occasionally, kill small antelopes, hares, rodents, birds and smaller monkeys (Goffe and Fischer, 2016; Swedell, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Analysis of mitochondrial DNA yields a phylogeny where baboon haplogroups reflect geographic origin better than external phenotypes or taxonomic classification.
source: Analysis of mitochondrial DNA yields a phylogeny that includes several major haplogroups or clades – groups of individuals who belong to a specific mitochondrial lineage. These haplogroups reflect the geographic origin of the respective specimens better than their external phenotypes or taxonomic classification, making species appear to be paraphyletic and polyphyletic when mapped onto the mitochondrial phylogeny (Zinner et al., 2009; Zinner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to genetic studies.

claim: Whole genome sequence comparisons confirm the six baboon species taxonomy.
source: Comparisons of whole genome sequences confirm the six baboon species taxonomy and suggest that the initial evolutionary divergence separated a southern lineage that ultimately produced Kinda, chacma and yellow baboons, from a northern lineage that produced olive, hamadryas and Guinea baboons (Rogers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to genomic analysis.

claim: The initial evolutionary divergence separated a southern lineage (Kinda, chacma and yellow baboons) from a northern lineage (olive, hamadryas and Guinea baboons).
source: Comparisons of whole genome sequences confirm the six baboon species taxonomy and suggest that the initial evolutionary divergence separated a southern lineage that ultimately produced Kinda, chacma and yellow baboons, from a northern lineage that produced olive, hamadryas and Guinea baboons (Rogers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Ancient hybridization events appear to have affected the genetic makeup of all baboon species.
source: Ancient hybridization events appear to have affected the genetic makeup of all species.

claim: Guinea baboons most likely experienced genetic admixture with a 'ghost lineage' that is probably extinct or not represented in analyzed genome samples.

claim: Multiple episodes of admixture and introgression in baboons have been linked to climate change and range expansion.

claim: Similar evolutionary mechanisms including gene transfer by introgressive hybridization influenced the evolution of Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans.

claim: The absence of genomic data from non-sapiens African hominins hinders the ability to ask questions about ancestral African hominin hybridization.

claim: Baboons allow us to study the impact of gene flow in an extant model.

claim: Baboons have been subject to recurrent range shifts, fragmentation, and isolation and reconnection of populations.

claim: Group size in chacma, olive and yellow baboons ranges from about a dozen up to roughly one hundred animals.
